catalog_quote: Katuic languages are phonologically typical Austroasiatic languages of the lower Mekong region with prosodic words of a maximally disyllabic, iambic template and vowel inventories with nine to eleven vowel qualities (Gehrmann and Conver 2015, Jenny et al. 2015). ... PK words may be monosyllables or disyllables. The final syllable or main syllable of a disyllabic word is always prosodically prominent and phonotactically unrestricted while the penultimate syllable or presyllable is always unstressed and phonotactically restricted with respect to the main syllable. A monosyllable is by definition a main syllable without a presyllable and, therefore, phonotactically equivalent to the main syllable of a disyllabic word. ... The PK phonological word is a maximally disyllabic iamb (cf. Butler 2015a) but not a sesquisyllable in the original sense of the word as coined by Matisoff (1973).
world_status: accessible description is silent on stress

The final syllable or main syllable of a disyllabic word is always prosodically prominent and phonotactically unrestricted while the penultimate syllable or presyllable is always unstressed and phonotacticall…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are at most disyllabic; the final (main) syllable carries the stress and the presyllable is unstressed. This is a family-wide (Katuic) and Proto-Katuic statement, not a description of Lower Ta'oih itself; the only first-hand tto data in print (L-Thongkum 2002, pp. 98-101, broad phonetic transcription) mark primary stress on the final syllable of every disyllable (taˈpat 'six', kaˈcaŋ 'to smile', ŋˈhaaŋ 'bone', parˈʔaw 'thigh'), consistent with the family pattern, but give no rule in prose.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not mentioned (Gehrmann 2018); no marks in L-Thongkum 2002.
new_statements.exceptions: Gehrmann 2018 p. 138: 'The description of the PK word above does not accurately describe the prosodic word of any one modern Katuic language' -- said of presyllable structure (reduction, sesquisyllabification), not of stress placement. Ta'oiq is listed among languages whose presyllable coda nasals have been reanalysed as prenasalised onsets (Table 8, p. 138).
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word (maximally disyllabic iamb); citation-form wordlist items in L-Thongkum 2002. Gehrmann's Ta'oiq data (Conver, Conver & Schmutz ms.) is labelled [tth] although Gehrmann & Conver 2015 equate Ta'oiq with the Ong/Ir/Katang type that Glottolog files with tto; the tto-specific evidence is therefore only L-Thongkum's Tha Taeng transcriptions.
new_statements.identity_note: Lower Ta'oih [tto] = lowe1395, filed by Glottolog 5.1 under Katuic > Ta'oi > Ong beside Ong-Ir [oog] (ongg1239); Ethnologue alternate name Tong, dialects Tong and Hantong' (quoted in Schmutz 2013: viii). Glottolog's bibliography equates L-Thongkum's 'Ta Oi' of Tha Taeng' (Sekong) with tto, and Gehrmann & Conver 2015 (p. lvi) describe the Ong/Ir/Katang-type Ta'oi ('Ta'oiq', a register language restructuring final stops) as one of the two main Ta'oi languages, which fits L-Thongkum's post-glottalised Ta Oi'. Gehrmann 2018 nevertheless codes his Ta'oiq data (Conver, Conver & Schmutz ms., Champasak) as [tth]. Upper Ta'oih [tth] = uppe1406 (van der Haak 1993 Ta'uaih; Vietnamese Ta-oih of Solntseva 1996 and Nguyen Van Loi 1986, which Gehrmann & Conver place with Pacoh) is a different entity; nothing quoted here comes from those tth sources. Huffman's 1971 Ta-Oi notebook informant (Tasseng Huay Hee, Salavan) is of undetermined variety.

tone_statements.citation: Gehrmann, Ryan. 2015. Vowel height and register assignment in Katuic. Journal of the Southeast Asian Linguistics Society 8: 56-70. Canberra: Asia-Pacific Linguistics. hdl:1885/16488
tone_statements.quote: Ta’oiq (sub-varieties of which are called Ong, Ir and Katang) has a tense-marked register system (tense register: creaky phonation) that is contrastive for all vowels excepting close central vowels, which are always lax. The tense register has also regularly conditioned consonantal restructuring ... resulting in a series of glottalized final consonants. Ta’uas (also called Ta’oih) does not have vocalic register contrast but does have glottalized finals in cognate etyma indicating that the most recent common ancestor of Ta’oiq and Ta’uas, Proto-Ta’oi (PT) was a tense-marked register language with altered final consonants.
tone_statements.summary: No tone; Ta'oiq: 2 registers (creaky/tense vs modal) + glottalized codas; Ta'uas (Ta'oih): no register, glottalized finals only.

tone.quote: Ta’oiq contrasts modal vs. non-modal phonation types at two different phases in the rime duration. Rime-medially, half-way through the rime duration, we find unpredictable variation of modal voice and creaky voice. Rime-finally, we find a three-way phonation contrast of modal voiced, glottalized and voiceless. … Checked terminance is interpreted here as a feature of coda consonants rather than a suprasegmental in Ta’oiq. … As for the two vowel phonation patterns, these are most readily interpreted as properties of the vowel
tone.locator: sec. 4.3 'Laryngeal Features of the Ta’oiq Rime', p. 7 (opening paragraph) and p. 9 (last two paragraphs of 4.3)
tone.summary: No tone system described: Ta’oiq has modal vs creaky vowels and voiced/glottalized/voiceless rime endings, analysed as vowel and coda features, not suprasegmentals; said not to be a register language.
tone.says: No tone system described: Ta’oiq has modal vs creaky vowels and voiced/glottalized/voiceless rime endings, analysed as vowel and coda features, not suprasegmentals; said not to be a register language.

sources.citation: Gehrmann, Ryan. 2022. Desegmentalization: towards a common framework for the modeling of tonogenesis and registrogenesis in mainland Southeast Asia with case studies from Austroasiatic. PhD thesis (Linguistics), University of Edinburgh. ix+126 pp. hdl:1842/39113
sources.note: Two-way rime register, creaky vs. clear (series A/B), plus post-glottalised finals, described as phonation with no pitch values; creakiness equated with Ferlus's Ong 'glottal tone'; Lao loans toneless.

tone.quote: In Talan, as in Ong and in the same etyma, there is a full series of post-glottalised continuants in word final position … contrasting with plain ones … There is also a full series of creaky? final rimes … Postglottalisation and creakiness do not co-occur. … Creakiness corresponds to what Ferlus (1974) calls the Ong "glottal tone". In any case, this set of creaky final continuants is in phonological contrast wit the postglottalised, and with the plain final continuants. … Lao borrowings, which are not as numerous here as in so other Katuic languages, are pronounced without tones
tone.locator: p. 140, KATUIC section and notes 3-4, p. 150

sources.citation: Gehrmann, Ryan. 2019. On the origin of rime laryngealization in Ta'oiq: a case study in the phonatory restructuring of vowel quality contrasts. Paper presented at the 8th International Conference on Austroasiatic Linguistics (ICAAL 8), Chiang Mai University, Chiang Mai, Thailand, 29-31 August 2019.
sources.note: No tone contrast is described: a high rising-falling pitch accompanies post-glottalised final consonants, which the author reads as possible incipient tonogenesis in a non-tonal language.

tone.quote: … the PEK finals *-p, *- t, and *-c in some words have become post-glottalised -m?, -nt, -j? in Ta Oi' … I have not heard any pre-gottalised final nasals in the speech of my Chatong and Ta Oi' informants. In fact, a high-rising-falling pitch always accompanies the post-glottalisation in Ta Oi' and Chatong. I suspect that both pre- and post-glottalisation are perhaps part of the process of 'a non-tonal language becoming tonal'. Moreover, I think that Chatong and Ta Oi', which are spoken by hundreds of people, belong to the Yir-Ong-Ta Oih or Katang-Ta Oih group of the East Katuic sub-branch.
tone.locator: p. 101, sec. 4 'Katuic languages', paragraph following the Ta Oi' post-glottalised word list

sources.citation: Diffloth, Gérard. 1989. Proto-Austroasiatic creaky voice. Mon-Khmer Studies 15: 139-154.
sources.note: Classifies Ta'oiq (with Sedang and Chongic) as a tense-marked register language - low register modal, high register laryngealized/creaky - whose register is cognate with vowel-quality (height) contrasts in related Katuic languages, not with proto onset voicing (pKatuic voiced stops devoiced with no registral reflex); sec. 4.10-4.10.2 (pp. 81-84) 'Sedang Variant of the Chong Model', Table 91 'Modern Ta'oiq reflexes of pKatuic rimes' (high register lenites coda *p *t *c *k to mˀ nˀ jˀ ʔ with shift to low register; post-glottalized nasals after short vowels); p. 99 treats this as resegmentalizat…

tone.quote: There are also tense-marked register languages, in which it is the low register that is characterized by unmarked modal phonation while the high register is accompanied by marked laryngealization or creak.17 [fn. 17: e.g. Sedang (< Bahnaric < Austroasiatic) ... and Ta’oiq (< Katuic < Austroasiatic) (Ferlus 1974a; Diffloth 1989; Gehrmann 2015, 2019)] ... In Ta’oiq, we find coda consonant mutations rather than deletions under the creaky high register (Ferlus 1974a, Diffloth 1989, Gehrmann 2019). pKatuic coda oral stops lenite to glottalized sonorants or a simple glottal stop segment in the case of coda *-k with accompanying shift to low register.
tone.locator: p. 12 with fn. 17 (ch. 2) and p. 84 in sec. 4.10.2 'Coda Deletions and Coda Mutations in Tense-Marked Register Languages' (sec. 4.10 = 'The Chong Model (OP + VH + CP)', pp. 81-84); resegmentalization passage p. 99
tone.summary: Ta'oiq: tense-marked 2-register system (modal low vs creaky high), partly resegmentalized as glottalized codas; no tone.
